definition: Radiation whose individual photons or particles carry enough energy (conventionally about 10 eV or more) to knock electrons out of atoms or molecules.
The conventional boundary between non-ionizing and ionizing photons, about 10 eV (124 nm, far ultraviolet). Different standards place it between 10 and 33 eV.
Chemical change caused by absorbing a photon that rearranges bonds without removing an electron. UV-B sunburn is photochemistry, not ionization.
A defect in which two adjacent thymine bases on one DNA strand become chemically bonded after absorbing UV light, kinking the DNA and blocking copying.
A helium nucleus (two protons, two neutrons, charge +2) emitted by some radioactive nuclei. It ionizes densely and is stopped by paper or the outer layer of skin.
A fast electron (or positron) emitted by a nucleus. It travels a few millimeters in tissue and is stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum or plastic.
A high-energy photon emitted by an atomic nucleus. It is physically the same as an X-ray of the same energy; only the origin differs.
Free neutrons, which carry no charge, pass easily through heavy materials, are slowed most effectively by collisions with hydrogen nuclei, and can make materials radioactive.
Atomic nuclei from outside the solar system moving near light speed: about 85% protons, 14% helium nuclei, and 1% heavier (HZE) nuclei.
A highly reactive molecular fragment with an unpaired electron, such as the hydroxyl radical (•OH) formed when radiation ionizes water. It causes most X-ray and gamma-ray DNA damage.
SI unit of absorbed dose: one joule of radiation energy deposited per kilogram of material (1 Gy = 100 rad).
SI unit of equivalent or effective dose: absorbed dose multiplied by weighting factors for radiation type (and, for effective dose, organ sensitivity). 1 Sv = 100 rem.
A multiplier w_R that converts gray to sievert: 1 for photons and electrons, 2 for protons, 20 for alpha particles and heavy ions, and 2.5–20 for neutrons depending on energy.
For a point source with no absorption, intensity falls as 1/r² because the same energy spreads over a sphere of area 4πr².
The fraction of photons removed per unit thickness of a material (μ, in cm⁻¹), so that intensity falls as I = I₀e^(−μx). It equals the mass attenuation coefficient times density.
The thickness of a material that cuts a photon beam's intensity in half, equal to ln 2 / μ.
The magnetic force F = qv × B on a moving charge. It is perpendicular to the velocity, so it bends the path without changing the speed.
The radius r = mv/(qB) of the circle or helix a charged particle traces in a magnetic field, using the velocity component perpendicular to the field.
The region around a planet controlled by its magnetic field, bounded by the magnetopause, which deflects most solar-wind particles around the planet.
Two doughnut-shaped zones of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field: an inner belt dominated by protons and an outer belt dominated by electrons.
